transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Nina Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Hannah Cole (Redwood CSM), Olivia Chen (StellarPay Lead Eng), Samir Patel (Product), Luis Romero (SRE), Aisha Khan (Security)
---
[00:00] Nina Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, it looks like we have most of the team. Quick agenda, Marcus will demo the updated SDK pattern for structured output and function orchestration, we'll review regression results Olivia ran, then security questions and next steps, okay?
[00:20] Olivia Chen: Yep that's good, we have some failures in the structured output tests I wanted to highlight.
[00:34] Marcus Li: Cool, I'll share screen, give me one sec. The gist is we've added a JSON schema enforcement example and a thin validator that runs right after the model emits partial streaming tokens so you can reject and retry heuristically.
[00:50] Samir Patel: When you say "reject and retry" is that automatic? I mean we don't want a UX hiccup for the agent in the app.
[01:05] Marcus Li: Right, it's configurable. The SDK provides a validateSchema hook; default behavior is to attempt a single automatic repair attempt using constrained prompts, then fall back to returning the partial payload with a validation error flag. You can flip to synchronous strict mode which will retry up to N times before returning an error.
[01:30] Olivia Chen: We're seeing a lot of fields come back as strings when they should be arrays or numbers, especially in edge cases where the prompt contains punctuation. It fails our client-side parser and crashes.
[01:45] Marcus Li: That sounds like tokenization-induced type coercion — we saw similar with long lists where the model emits natural-language commas. The SDK example we pushed last night includes an explicit type-casting pass and an allowlist of canonical tokens for enums.
[02:10] Luis Romero: Quick ops question: if you do streaming with function calling, do partial function outputs get cached in the KV cache? We worry about duplicate side-effects if we re-invoke during retry.
[02:25] Marcus Li: Good call. The runtime's KV cache is prefix-only for completed steps; partial streams aren't written to persistent KV until the function call completes successfully. If you re-issue a function-call we recommend idempotency keys for external side-effects. I'll add a snippet to the SDK docs.
[02:50] Aisha Khan: From security: can you confirm the pilot will keep logs for 90 days and that PII is redacted, and where is the KMS? We need to know if the KMS is customer-managed or Redwood-managed for the Private deployment.
[03:10] Nina Patel: For hosted pilot defaults we keep logs for 30 days, but for Dedicated/Private we can extend retention and integrate with customer KMS (bring-your-own). Hannah will follow up with the SOC2 scoping and the KMS playbook.
[03:30] Hannah Cole: I'll upload the scoping doc later today. For the pilot we can run in a Private VPC with customer-managed KMS, and audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[03:48] Samir Patel: Thanks. Back to structured output: Olivia, can you walk us through the failing sample?
[04:01] Olivia Chen: Sure. Example one — we ask for a list of transaction suggestions as an array of objects with keys (id:int, label:str, score:float). The model returns a top-level object with a human explanation then the array. Our parser chokes because the overall type isn't exactly the array we expect.
[04:25] Marcus Li: That's a classic wrapper problem. Two mitigations: change the schema to accept {result: array} or add a post-processing extractor that finds the first JSON blob matching the schema. Our SDK includes an extractor with fuzzy matching heuristics but it's turned off by default to avoid masking real regressions.
[04:50] Olivia Chen: Fuzzy matching hides bugs though. We prefer stricter fails in CI but a permissive mode in prod with monitoring.
[05:05] Marcus Li: Agreed — we've added a 'ciStrict' flag so your CI runs with strict parsing and prod toggles to permissive but increments a metric for every rewrite.
[05:20] [05:20] Marcus Li screen share: walking through code snippet...
[06:05] Marcus Li: Here is the function-calling flow. You define a function signature in the SDK, the runtime serializes arguments and calls the function. When streaming, the SDK buffers tokens and only invokes the function when the signature is complete or when a stop token appears.
[06:30] Olivia Chen: How do we handle ambiguous completions that look like a function call but are missing fields?
[06:45] Marcus Li: The SDK has a preflight check — it will run lightweight parsing to confirm required fields. If missing, it will either emit a partial call event to the app (you can handle partial) or it will request the model to fill missing fields using a short contextual prompt. That prompt is included in the same request so it stays within the per-request footprint.
[07:10] Samir Patel: Sounds good. About costs — streaming plus multiple retries will spike token usage. Nina, can you give us rough numbers for the pilot scale we discussed (50k requests/day, avg 150 tokens)?
[07:25] Nina Patel: On hosted pilot pricing, with streaming and two retry attempts, we'd estimate ~1.8x token usage versus a single-shot baseline. I'll send a spreadsheet with delta numbers. The Dedicated option will be more predictable; Private gives more control but has infra baseline.
[07:50] Aisha Khan: For compliance, if we go Private on-prem, is audit logging fully in-customer network? We need evidence for PCI scoping.
[08:05] Marcus Li: Yes, Private deployments can be fully air-gapped; audit logging is customer-configured and never sent to Redwood by default. For VPC-hosted Private we can integrate with CloudWatch/Stackdriver/Splunk — whatever your SIEM uses.
[08:25] Olivia Chen: Back to function orchestration — we tried orchestrating two function calls sequentially and saw a 500ms overhead per call plus some jitter. Any tips?
[08:40] Marcus Li: Sequential calls will cost you latency. If functions are independent, parallelize them using the SDK's parallel-call helper. For dependent flows, we recommend batching some inputs or using a single function that invokes internal microservices to reduce round trips. Also we have a 'warm' kernel pinning that can shave cold-start stalls.
[09:05] Luis Romero: Is kernel pinning available in Dedicated or only Hosted?
[09:12] Marcus Li: Both — but Dedicated gives more control over warm pools and TTLs. Kernel pinning here means keeping the compiled kernels resident on the GPU for models you designate. It reduces first-gen latency.
[09:30] [09:30] Olivia Chen: I've uploaded the regression artifacts to the shared folder. The pattern we see is mostly schema shape and some enum variations.
[09:44] Marcus Li: I'll open PR for the SDK that adds strict ci mode and an enum canonicalizer.
[10:00] Samir Patel: We also have a UX question — when the model returns a validation error mid-stream, should we show partial data with a warning or block UI update until repaired?
[10:14] Marcus Li: That depends on your product. The SDK leaves that to you but suggests showing a loading skeleton and a toast saying "partial results" with an action to retry. We can add a pre-built UX widget to the example repo if you'd like.
[10:30] Olivia Chen: That'd speed up our integration.
[10:35] [10:35] Hannah Cole: Quick note — we now have a design pattern doc for UIs handling streaming and partial outputs, will share link.
[10:45] Aisha Khan: Security again: KMS — if we hand over our own KMS keys, do you support HSM backed keys? We need to know for FIPS compliance.
[10:58] Nina Patel: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS including HSM-backed keys in Private deployments. Hosted will be Redwood-managed by default, but enterprise contracts allow customer KMS with proper key rotation. Hannah to provide details.
[11:20] [11:20] Marcus Li: Alright, showing the new SDK example now: it includes a small state machine for function orchestration, a validator that uses a JSON schema (draft-07), and a metrics emitter for validation failures. It also demonstrates how to surface partial function results to the app safely.
[11:45] Marcus Li: Note there's a transform hook so you can canonicalize field names (snake_case -> camelCase) before your parser runs.
[12:05] Olivia Chen: Will the canonicalizer affect latency much?
[12:15] Marcus Li: It's negligible; it's a small in-process transformation. The heavy parts are model calls and any networked function invocations.
[12:28] Samir Patel: About the validation failures counts — can Redwood push a metric to our Datadog?
[12:34] Hannah Cole: Yes, we support Datadog/Kibana/Splunk integrations. We can push events or you can pull via our metrics API.
[12:50] Luis Romero: We want to avoid duplicate side-effects if a retry occurs. You mentioned idempotency keys earlier — how robust is that approach with asynchronous webhooks?
[13:05] Marcus Li: Use stateless idempotency tokens and server-side dedupe. SDK adds a middleware to generate idempotency keys per function call and attach them to the outbound request; the webhook receiver needs to check those keys. For asynchronous flows, we recommend a two-phase commit pattern.
[13:30] Olivia Chen: For one of our flows we need to call an internal fraud scoring service during the function call. Latency is tight — sub-250ms. Any guidance?
[13:45] Marcus Li: If the scoring service is external, try a shadow call approach: call it in parallel, and if it returns in time, include results; otherwise proceed with a default. For hard constraints, move the critical scoring into a local microservice in the same VPC as the inference runtime to minimize hops.
[14:05] Samir Patel: Let's talk acceptance criteria for the pilot. We want <200ms p95 for simple suggestions and structured-output pass rate >95% in CI. Is that feasible?
[14:20] Nina Patel: For simple suggestion p95, on Dedicated it's feasible; on hosted pilot we can get close depending on model variant and batch tuning. Structured-output >95% in CI is ambitious but achievable with stricter prompts, schema enforcement, and client-side canonicalizers. We'll help tune prompts and batching profiles.
[14:45] [14:45] Olivia Chen: Any gotchas on tokenization with numbers/ids? We had an issue where long numeric IDs were split with spaces and then parsed as strings.
[14:58] Marcus Li: Use code-fence or backticks to force literal tokenization for IDs, and in the schema treat numeric IDs as strings if you can't guarantee encoding. Also we have a tokenizer-safe encoder in the SDK that preserves tokens for critical fields.
[15:15] Luis Romero: For the regression runs Olivia did, what's the recommended way to replay them against different revisions of the runtime?
[15:28] Marcus Li: We recommend capturing raw requests (prompt + metadata + seed) and re-running them with exact model version pinned. The SDK's test harness can replay with a fixed seed and deterministic sampling parameters.
[15:45] Olivia Chen: We've been seeing nondeterministic output even with low temp; is that expected?
[15:58] Marcus Li: With sampling set to deterministic (top_p=0, temp=0) it's much more deterministic, but some model architectures still have minor variability due to system-level nondeterminism. Pinning a model binary on Dedicated reduces that variability.
[16:18] Samir Patel: From product POV, we need a clear migration path from hosted pilot to Dedicated with minimal code changes. How stable are the SDK APIs?
[16:30] Marcus Li: The SDK maintains stable public APIs. Differences are mainly in configuration (endpoint, auth) and optional Dedicated knobs like kernel pinning. We provide a migration checklist.
[16:45] [16:45] Hannah Cole: I'll attach the checklist to the follow-up notes.
[17:00] Nina Patel: Ok quick recap and next steps: Marcus will open the SDK PR with ciStrict and enum canonicalizer; Olivia will upload failing cases; Hannah will share SOC2/KMS scoping; Nina will share pricing sheet. Target dates are in action items. Any final questions?
[17:20] Olivia Chen: No, thanks. Good progress.
[17:30] Samir Patel: Thanks all.
[17:40] Nina Patel: We'll follow up via email and Slack thread, and schedule next sync same time next week.
[17:46] End of call.

Notes on transcription: minor mis-hearings: "KV cache" appears as "KV cash" in one snippet, proper nouns sometimes mistranscribed (e.g., kernel pinning became 'kernel pinning' but pronounced oddly). Speaker overlap at ~10:30 caused some words to be clipped.
